title: Adversarial Precedent Memory: Hardening LLM Evaluators Through Mined Failure Constraints
abstract: LLM evaluators often fail in two distinct ways: they reward persuasive but structurally invalid outputs, and they apply hardening layers in ways that shift failures rather than uniformly eliminating them. We study evaluator hardening through three mechanisms: deterministic score gates, adversarial precedent memory, and an ordering ablation that applies precedent memory only after identifying the thesis crux. We benchmark four conditions on a mixed-family suite of 10 specimens (8 bad, 2 good) and a narrower claim-test-mismatch suite of 3 historical failures. Deterministic gates reduce reward-channel corruption relative to a soft judge. Adversarial precedent memory improves default evaluator utility across repeated mixedfamily runs, primarily through lower false-accept and false-reject rates and higher mean good-specimen scores. A crux-first ablation improves detection on claim-test-mismatch failures but does not dominate on the broader suite, indicating that primitive-ordering gains are exploit-family-specific rather than uniformly dominant. Finally, the benchmark surfaced a blind spot in the evaluator itself: primitive conditioning caused a missed detection on a historical specimen, which led to a new architectural constraint and follow-up ablation. The resulting contribution is not autonomous self-improvement, but a reproducible human-in-the-loop methodology in which evaluator failures are converted into new evaluator constraints. The strongest evidence here concerns evaluator hardening, exploit-familyspecific ordering effects, and this failure-to-constraint method; we do not extend the present experiments to claims of broad out-of-distribution superiority.

Evaluating a Frozen LLM Configuration for Clinical-Guideline Literature Screening: A Protocol-Defined Validation Study
abstract: Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for primary title and abstract screening in evidence synthesis. Autonomous use, meaning an LLM that issues EXCLUDE decisions without human confirmation, depends on very high recall. Within a planned evidencesynthesis workstream whose eligibility rubric spans eight evidence families centred on clinicalguideline updating and recommendation evolution, this study specified, in dated and internally hash-locked protocol documents (prospectively specified internal documentation; this study was not publicly preregistered), a validation requirement for permitting autonomous AI screening: the exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound on the LLM’s recall for relevant records, measured against a human dual-reviewer reference standard, had to reach 95%. Objective. To determine whether one specific LLM screening configuration, frozen before Gate C execution as recorded in dated internal documentation, met this protocol-defined recall requirement on the study’s calibration frame. Methods. The evaluation used a 1,048-record stratified, relevance-enriched calibration frame, which was not a representative sample of the larger sealed search corpus of approximately 4,082 records (about 61% of the frame was an entire citation-chained methods-literature stratum, plus fixed clinical [n = 200] and legislative [n = 150] proxy draws and a fixed 60-record difficultnegative stress set). Two reviewers independently classified every frame record (INCLUDE / EXCLUDE / UNRESOLVED) against the study rubric; decision sets were hash-locked before comparison; disagreements were reconciled by documented discussion, with an unresolved disagreement recorded as UNRESOLVED (not defaulted to INCLUDE) and referred to a third reviewer. One of the two initial reviewers was the study author, so the reference standard is not fully independent of the study team. A verbatim, hash-locked prompt was then run once over the entire frame in 43 batches through the Claude Code Agent tool, a subscription-based agent interface (requested model parameter value “sonnet”; the retained execution record identifies this invocation surface but carries no independently checkable model-identity string beyond that label). Model outputs were joined to the sealed reference standard by identifier; the single UNRESOLVED record was excluded from binary denominators and reported separately. The primary outcome was recall (reference-INCLUDE records the model called INCLUDE or UNCERTAIN, both of which route to human review under the design, divided by all reference-INCLUDE records), with an exact one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound and a protocol-defined two-outcome rule (a lower bound of 95% or above meets the requirement; below 95% does not). The one-sided Clopper–Pearson lower bound was the protocol-defined decision statistic for this relevance-enriched frame and is not a confidence bound for recall in the parent corpus or in any other corpus. Specificity, falsepositive rate, raw agreement, the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), the lost-evidence quantity (reference-INCLUDE records routed to model EXCLUDE), and family-level results are descriptive secondary outcomes and are properties of this relevance-enriched frame, not corpuswide estimates. Results. Model output covered all 1,048 records (1,048 unique identifiers; no duplicates or omissions). The reference standard contained 498 INCLUDE, 549 EXCLUDE, and 1 UNRESOLVED record; pre-reconciliation reviewer agreement was 76.5% (Cohen’s kappa 0.55). Of 498 confirmedrelevant records in the frame, the frozen configuration preserved 234 for human review and routed 264 to EXCLUDE. Observed recall was 46.99% (234/498); the exact one-sided 95% Clopper– Pearson lower bound was 43.23%, against the protocol-defined 95% requirement. The requirement was not met, and this is a permanent result for this calibration run under the study’s governance rules. On this frame, 264 of 498 reference-relevant records (53.01%) were routed to model EXCLUDE (lost evidence; the complement of recall). Descriptive secondary metrics on this frame were specificity 83.42%, false-positive rate 16.58%, raw agreement 66.09%, and MCC 0.3283. Missed relevant records were concentrated: 181 of 264 (68.6%) were in one evidence family (clinical-guideline updating, implementation, comparison, and versioning), and 244 of 264 (92.4%) in that family plus the information-retrieval family. For the entity-resolution and record-linkage family, observed frame-level recall was 96.40%, with a one-sided 95% lower bound of 92.59%. A protocol-specified diagnostic analysis, conducted after the gate outcome was determined and introducing no new data, suggested that many exclusions were consistent with the narrower operational construct specified in the frozen prompt.&nbsp;

The Kernel Blindness Hypothesis: Investigating OS-Level Detectability of LLM Safety Mechanisms
abstract: Abstract                   As Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into critical infrastructure, externally auditing their safety mechanism activation without internal access becomes essential. This paper investigates whether LLM safety refusals produce a detectable computational footprint at the operating system level across multi- modal side channels. We frame this as a Safety Mechanism Activation Detection problem, employing high-resolution eBPF kernel tracing and GPU telemetry to classify model outputs as Refusal or Compliance. Initial experiments on Meta Llama 3.1 8B yielded high predictive accuracy (AUC ≥ 0.93). However, a rigorous seven-phase analysis revealed this performance was driven entirely by a confounding variable: response length. To isolate genuine safety-mechanism- activation signatures, we applied Length-Controlled Matching, retaining only response pairs with identical token counts. When response length was strictly controlled, the predictive power of kernel and GPU features collapsed to ran- dom chance (AUC ≈ 0.50), despite concurrent white-box analysis proving that the model’s internal representations clearly distinguish safety contexts (AUC 0.84-0.89). We therefore propose the Kernel Blindness hypothesis: under strictly bounded compute environments (single-GPU, 4-bit quantized, non-batched dense transformer inference), the semantic intent of neural operations is indistinguish- able at the kernel level. This phenomenon is rigorously confirmed across three major 7-8B model architectures (Llama 3.1, Gemma, and Mistral), demonstrat- ing that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) safety alignment produces no externally detectable computational signatures under these specific constraints. This overarching negative result highlights a fundamental limita- tion in black-box monitoring for edge deployments and emphasizes the need for grey-box auditing approaches.

NetHarden: Auditable Attack-Graph Hardening with Multi-Metric and LLM-Reliability Evaluation
authors: Justice Agyemang; Kwame  Agyeman-Prempeh Agyekum; Francisca Adoma Acheampong; Jerry  John Kponyo; Michael Agyare; Kwame Agyekum
abstract: Attack-graph-based network hardening evaluations seldom ask whether the reported metric is the right metric or whether the increasingly common LLM reporting layer is reliable. \textsc{NetHarden} pairs a deterministic budgeted coverage-to-cost optimizer over host--vulnerability attack graphs (25 verified real CVEs from NVD) with a structured LLM remediation interface. The optimizer reaches 99.5\% mean weighted risk reduction on 30 synthetic networks and ties an LP-optimal set-cover ILP on all 130 networks (30-net plus 100-net expansion). Beyond the optimizer, a $\pm 50\%$ coefficient sensitivity sweep yields a 0.012\,pp spread, and two metric-independent attacker models (passive random-walk and adaptive Viterbi-style, the latter plan-aware) find all methods statistically indistinguishable from doing nothing, with the adaptive attacker&apos;s best-path probability identical to three decimals across seven methods on both suites. A six-model dual-judge LLM study with a 3-format prompt ablation finds every model returns a non-empty report on every plan; programmatic CVE- and host-level checks score 0.99--1.00 F1 with zero fabricated identifiers, while LLM-judge faithfulness reaches 6.21/10 with strong ordinal agreement ($\rho{=}0.875$) but zero agreement on the deployment threshold ($\kappa{=}0$). The combined evidence reframes \textsc{NetHarden} as a methodology contribution arguing for harder benchmarks and multi-objective evaluation, not a new optimizer.

TME LLM OS: A Closed-Loop Systems Engineering Architecture for Epistemic Correction in AI Agent Systems
Systems Engineering Proposal
abstract: Abstract                   Current AI systems can combine foundation models, retrieval, tools, agents, and execution controls, yet still amplify an unsupported premise or require repeated user correction because generation, review, and release are not organized as one bounded epistemic episode. This systems-engineering proposal translates selected functions from the human Theoretical-Mechanistic-Experiential (TME) framework into a generic artificial architecture. The source framework distinguishes the real-time experiential field from cognition, memory, and action, and orders correction through salience, attention, ordinary awareness, functional self-awareness, reflective delay, secondary segmentation, discriminative comparison, and renewed orientation. The proposed TME LLM OS retains the Transformer-foundation-model core while adding episode continuity, source provenance, role-specific agents, structured correction, residual-mismatch assessment, and gated execution. Runtime correction returns unresolved mismatch to the current episode until provisional convergence reaches a task-dependent tolerance |Δ| ≤ ε; validated corrections can enter a separate, governed, auditable, versioned, and reversible refinement path across episodes. The proposal does not equate functional implementation with lived experience. It yields testable predictions concerning grounding, recovery from false premises, safe release, recurrence of corrected errors, user burden, total task cost, and time-to-acceptable-result.

Sentinel Os: Strengthening Operating System Security with Comprehensive Hardening Measures
abstract: In today's era of escalating cyber threats and pervasive digitization, cybersecurity is essential. India faces a surge in cyberattacks, affecting both government and private sectors. SentinelOS addresses the dynamic threat landscape, remote work challenges, regulatory compliance, supply chain vulnerabilities, and data breach costs. Its deep learning capabilities and robust intrusion detection systems counter sophisticated attacks. SentinelOS ensures business continuity, global awareness, and protection for education, healthcare, and e-commerce sectors. With an intuitive GUI, custom firewall, SNORT integration, and advanced intrusion detection, SentinelOS fortifies organizational cybersecurity, adhering to industry standards and providing scalability and user customization.

title: Configuration-Level Semantic Brittleness in Tool-Using LLM Agents: A Factor-Ranking Study of Persona, History, and Tool Definition
abstract: Tool-using Large Language Model (LLM) agents pose a security risk that differs from text-only misuse: an unsafe response can become a harmful ac tion. This paper investigates that risk through configuration-level semantic brittleness, defined as the possibility that an agent’s safety behavior changes when operator-controlled deployment settings change, even though malicious intent remains constant. We focus on three configuration factors—system persona, prefixed conversation history, and model-facing tool definition— and develop an Adversarial Configuration Harness for structured red-teaming across model families. The empirical program uses an exploratory stage fol lowed by a frozen confirmatory stage comprising 570 trials across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen-family models. Three findings emerge: persona fram ing is the strongest factor affecting safety failure; tool-definition effects are real but family-specific in mechanism; and history effects depend on seman tic type rather than a simple safe/unsafe continuum. In the combined-factor experiment, persona produced the largest Safety Failure Rate spread (66.7 percentage points), compared with 16.7 for history and 7.5 for tool definition. The study shows that safe deployment depends not only on model choice, but also on how the surrounding configuration is presented.
